title: Smoothness descends along arbitrary qcqs affine-transition limits
statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty directed set and $(S_i)_{i\in I}$ an inverse system of schemes with affine transition morphisms [def-pc-scheme] [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] [pqf-def-affine-morphism], and let $S=\varprojlim_iS_i$ [lem-weil-pbc-limit-affine-transition]. Fix $i_0\in I$ and assume $S_{i_0}$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Fix quasi-compact quasi-separated $S_{i_0}$-schemes $X_{i_0},Y_{i_0}$, and an $S_{i_0}$-morphism $f_{i_0}:X_{i_0}\to Y_{i_0}$ locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Write $f_i$ and $f$ for its base changes to $S_i$ and $S$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. If $f$ is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], there is $i\geq i_0$ such that $f_j$ is smooth for every $j\geq i$. No Noetherian hypothesis is imposed on the stages.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, in Situation situation-descent-property; persistence by base change of smooth morphisms

proof.text: Write $0=i_0$. For every $x\in X_0$, choose an affine open $W_x\subseteq S_0$ containing its image, an affine open $V_x\subseteq Y_0$ containing $f_0(x)$ and contained in the inverse image of $W_x$, and an affine open $U_x\subseteq X_0$ containing $x$ and contained in $f_0^{-1}(V_x)$. The affine-basis statement supplies each choice inside the specified open. The $U_x$ cover $X_0$, so quasi-compactness gives a finite subcover. Relabel its triples $(W_a,V_a,U_a)$ for $a\in A$, with $A$ finite. If $X_0$ is empty take $A$ empty. No assertion that intersections of affine opens are affine is needed.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, proof: affine-local reduction and Tag 0C0B

proof.text: For a fixed triple and $k\geq0$, put $W_k=S_k\times_{S_0}W_0$, $V_k=V_0\times_{W_0}W_k$, and $U_k=U_0\times_{W_0}W_k$; use analogous notation without subscripts over $S$. A morphism to $X_k$ whose image lies in the inverse image of $U_0$ factors uniquely through that open; its component to $X_0$ factors uniquely through $U_0$. The fibre-product universal property therefore identifies that open with $U_0\times_{S_0}S_k$, and likewise for $V_0$ and over $S$. The last two are precisely the inverse images of $V_0$ and $U_0$ in $Y_k$ and $X_k$: in both descriptions a test scheme gives the same pair of maps to the original open and to $S_k$, agreeing in $S_0$. The restricted morphism is $h_k:U_k\to V_k$. Projections $S_k\to S_0$ and $S\to S_0$ are affine. Affine permanence under base change makes $W_k,W,V_k,V,U_k,U$ affine, and their transition maps affine. The original ring map $B_0=\Gamma(V_0,\mathcal O)\to C_0=\Gamma(U_0,\mathcal O)$ is finitely presented by the affine-open finite-presentation lemma applied to $f_0$.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, proof: affine-local reduction and Tag 0C0B

proof.text: The restricted diagram $(W_k)_{k\geq0}$ has limit $W$, by the open-limit clause of the affine-transition theorem. The diagram $(V_k)$ has limit $V$: a compatible cone $T\to V_k$ gives a single $T\to V_0$ and a compatible cone $T\to W_k$ agreeing over $W_0$; the latter gives a unique $T\to W$, hence a unique $T\to V_0\times_{W_0}W=V$. Conversely the two projections of this fibre product give the cone. Apply the affine limit formula to get $B=\Gamma(V,\mathcal O)=\varinjlim_{k\geq0}B_k$, where $B_k=\Gamma(V_k,\mathcal O)$, with the canonical ring coprojections. Pullback pasting gives $U_k=U_0\times_{V_0}V_k$ and $U=U_0\times_{V_0}V$: both pairs of maps agree in $V_0$, and their composite agreement in $W_0$ is exactly the defining agreement for the original fibre products. The affine-spectra fibre-product statement therefore identifies their rings, compatibly with both projections, as $C_k=C_0\otimes_{B_0}B_k$ and $C=C_0\otimes_{B_0}B$. Thus the diagram used in ring descent is the directed system of the $B_k$, not an unspecified system of rings.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, proof: affine-local reduction and Tag 0C0B

proof.text: The limit restriction $h:U\to V$ is smooth: $U,V$ are open subschemes of $X,Y$ and $f(U)\subseteq V$, so apply smooth restriction. Identify $h$ with the spectrum of $B\to C$ using the induced-ring-map spectrum square and the canonical affine-open isomorphisms; the smooth ring-map/affine-scheme equivalence gives smoothness of $B\to C$. Apply the fixed-map smooth-pushout descent theorem with its $A=B_0$, its $B=C_0$, diagram $F_k=B_k$, and pushouts $C_k=C_0\otimes_{B_0}B_k$, $L=C_0\otimes_{B_0}B$. Its finite-presentation hypothesis is exactly the one verified in step 2, and its smoothness hypothesis is the preceding equivalence. It gives an index $k_a\geq0$ where $B_{k_a}\to C_{k_a}$ is smooth. No Noetherian or faithful-flatness hypothesis occurs in this ring theorem.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, proof: affine-local reduction and Tag 0C0B

proof.text: By directedness choose an upper bound $i$ for the finite set consisting of $0$ and the indices $k_a$. This follows by induction on the finite set using a common upper bound for each pair; including $0$ handles $A=\varnothing$. For each $a$, the ring map $B_i\to C_i$ is the base change of $B_{k_a}\to C_{k_a}$: $U_{k_a}\times_{V_{k_a}}V_i$ and $U_i$ are both canonically $U_0\times_{V_0}V_i$. On test schemes this identifies the common map to $U_0$ and the map to $V_i$ agreeing in $V_0$, and preserves the projection to $V_i$. Affine fibre products thus identify the map with $B_i\to C_{k_a}\otimes_{B_{k_a}}B_i$. Smooth ring maps are stable under base change, so it is smooth. The affine-scheme equivalence, the spectrum square, and invariance under affine comparison isomorphisms give smoothness of $h_{a,i}:U_{a,i}\to V_{a,i}$. Composing with the open inclusion $V_{a,i}\to Y_i$ is smooth by clause (b) of smooth restriction.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, proof: affine-local reduction and Tag 0C0B

proof.text: The opens $U_{a,i}$ cover $X_i$: their union is the inverse image of $\bigcup_aU_{a,0}=X_0$ under $X_i\to X_0$. Each restricted composite to $Y_i$ was proved smooth in step 5. The source-local smoothness criterion now gives smoothness of $f_i$. The criterion also covers the empty family when $X_i=\varnothing$.

source.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth, proof: affine-local reduction and Tag 0C0B

proof.text: For every $j\geq i$, the canonical square from $f_j$ to $f_i$ is cartesian: $X_j=X_i\times_{Y_i}Y_j$, since both sides represent the pair of maps to $X_0$ and $S_j$ agreeing in $S_0$. Thus $f_j$ is the base change of $f_i$ along $Y_j\to Y_i$, and clause (2) of proper-and-smooth base change makes it smooth. This gives the all-later conclusion.

source.place: Tag 01VB, label lemma-base-change-smooth; applied to the cartesian square identified by the fibre-product universal property

proof_origin.place: Tag 0C0C, label lemma-descend-smooth; omitted affine-local reduction written out, with Tag 0C0B in algebra.tex and persistence Tag 01VB in morphisms.tex
